Ludlow
LUD-loh
n. (the Shropshire castle town that was the seat of the Council in the Marches of Wales, the court through which Wales was governed for a century and a half)
Old English hlūde hlāw, the hill by the loud water, from hlūd, loud, and hlāw, a hill or mound.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ludlow is the Shropshire town above the Teme, built round a Norman castle that became the administrative capital of Wales. The Council in the Marches of Wales sat there from the late fifteenth century, given statutory footing under Henry VIII and presided over by a Lord President; it exercised both judicial and executive power over Wales and the border shires, and for a century and a half the ordinary Welshman's experience of royal government was a summons to Ludlow. Prince Arthur kept court there and died there in 1502; Mary Tudor was sent there as a child. The council was abolished in 1689. Two things in its record concern the dictionary. The first is that its jurisdiction, being prerogative rather than common law, was a standing grievance: it fined, imprisoned and bound over on its own authority, and the Long Parliament struck at it along with Star Chamber. The second is that Richard Baxter, as a youth, was placed in the household of the council's chaplain at Ludlow and saw the court at close quarters, and recorded in his own account the looseness of the place. The dictionary holds the magistrate's office to be of God and its abuse to be judged by the same word that establishes it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a council as an assembly for consultation; a magistrate as a public civil officer; prerogative as an exclusive privilege; jurisdiction as legal authority; and justice as the giving to every man his due.

expand to see more

COUNCIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.

MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.

PREROGATIVE, n. An exclusive or peculiar privilege; an antecedent and exclusive right.

JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing the laws.

JUSTICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every man what is his due; conformity to the law.

Pro 29:2 — "When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn."

Mic 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Modern Corruption

Shropshire castle town and seat of the Council in the Marches of Wales, a prerogative court that governed Wales for a century and a half until the Long Parliament struck at its jurisdiction.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the prerogative court, a tribunal deriving its power from the sovereign's will rather than from law, and the dictionary names it as a corruption of the magistrate's office and not as its mere excess. Scripture gives the magistrate a sword and gives it to him for a defined end: “he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil” (Rom 13:4). A minister of God with a commission has a rule to answer to; a court that makes its own rule as it goes has the sword without the commission. The consequence is the one Solomon states, that the character of rulers is felt in the mood of a whole people, for “when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2).

The second word is against the other error, which is to conclude from the abuse that the office is worthless. The dictionary does not take the step. What is required of the man who holds the sword is stated and it is not complicated: “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God” (Mic 6:8). The measure of a government is not its efficiency in reducing a province but the righteousness by which it is itself governed, since “Righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34). Richard Baxter, set down in that household as a boy, drew from it a lifelong distrust of courts and a lifelong insistence that rulers are under law; the dictionary reckons both lessons sound.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mashal (H4910), to bear rule; Greek diakonos (G1249), a minister or servant; Hebrew mishpat (H4941), judgment or justice.

expand to see more

Hebrew mashal (H4910) — to rule, to have dominion; “but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn”, Proverbs 29:2.

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant, a minister; “he is the minister of God, a revenger”, Romans 13:4.

Greek machaira (G3162) — a sword, the instrument of civil execution; “he beareth not the sword in vain”, Romans 13:4.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, a verdict; “but to do justly, and to love mercy”, Micah 6:8.

Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness; “Righteousness exalteth a nation”, Proverbs 14:34.

Usage

"“he beareth not the sword in vain” (Rom 13:4) — the Council in the Marches and its prerogative jurisdiction."

"“when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn” (Pro 29:2) — a summons to Ludlow as the ordinary face of government."

"“Righteousness exalteth a nation” (Pro 14:34) — Baxter's judgment on the household he was placed in."
